items.stem: Read an extract written in a nineteenth-century style, ‘The House at Thornleigh’. ‘It was upon a raw evening in the latter part of November that I first beheld the house at Thornleigh. The coach, which had laboured since noon along roads more fit for ducks than horses, set me down at the gate and departed with indecent haste, as though the driver had no wish to linger. I confess that my spirits sank. Before me rose a long, low dwelling of grey stone, its windows shuttered, its chimneys smokeless, and about it a garden so overgrown that the very paths had been swallowed up. I had been promised a cheerful household and a warm welcome; I perceived neither. Yet I had come too far to turn back, and, gathering my cloak about me, I advanced towards the door.’ How does the writer create a mysterious and unwelcoming atmosphere in this extract? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Raw November evening; driver’s indecent haste; shuttered windows and smokeless chimneys; personified garden swallowing paths; contrast of promised welcome with reality; long formal sentences and the narrator’s sinking spirits.

items.stem: Read a letter written in a nineteenth-century style, from Charlotte to her sister. ‘My dearest Eliza, You will forgive, I hope, the shortness of this letter, for I write in great haste and by a failing candle. Mamma is much recovered, though the physician forbids her to venture out of doors until the weather mends. Our neighbour Mr Fenwick called upon us twice this week, and on the second occasion brought a basket of hothouse grapes, which Mamma declared to be very civil of him, and which I declared to be very sour. I am resolved to say no more of Mr Fenwick. Pray write soon and tell me all your news, for there is none here worth the telling. Your ever affectionate sister, Charlotte.’ What impressions of Charlotte and her life does the letter create? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Affectionate to her sister; witty and sharp (sour grapes); dutiful about Mamma; bored at home (no news worth telling); hidden feelings about Mr Fenwick; formal nineteenth-century conventions of address and sign-off.

items.stem: Read an extract from a story set in Vietnam, ‘The Lantern Festival’. ‘On the night of the full moon, the old town of Hoi An switched off its electric lights. Linh had seen it every year of her life, but it still made her catch her breath. One by one, the silk lanterns glowed into life along the riverbank, red and gold and green, until the water itself seemed to burn. Her grandmother pressed a paper lantern into her hands, a candle flickering inside. “Make a wish for someone else,” she said. “Wishes for yourself sink.” Linh thought of her father, working on a ship somewhere beyond the edge of the map, and set the lantern on the water. It wobbled, steadied, and drifted out to join the thousands of others, a slow river of light carrying everyone’s hopes towards the sea.’ How does the writer use the setting and cultural tradition to show Linh’s feelings? Support your answer with close reference to the text.
items.answer: Lantern festival as a communal tradition; magical light imagery; grandmother’s belief; father’s distance; the lantern’s journey mirrors Linh’s hope.

items.stem: Write a letter in a nineteenth-century style from Eliza replying to her sister Charlotte, using formal address, older vocabulary and longer sentences. Write about 350–450 words.
items.answer: Model approach: formal greeting and sign-off; archaic vocabulary (pray, resolved, civil); balanced, multi-clause sentences; witty response to the news about Mr Fenwick.

items.stem: Answer both parts. (a) Read this from an extract from a story set in Vietnam, ‘The Lantern Festival’: ‘“Make a wish for someone else,” she said. “Wishes for yourself sink.”’ What does Linh’s grandmother tell her to do? (b) Read this from an extract from a story set in Vietnam, ‘The Lantern Festival’: ‘Linh thought of her father, working on a ship’ Where is Linh’s father?
items.answer: (a) Make a wish for someone else (b) Working on a ship far away
items.markingKey: (a) Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘“Make a wish for someone else,” she said. “Wishes for yourself sink.”’). (b) Retrieval: the answer is stated in the quotation (‘Linh thought of her father, working on a ship’).

items.stem: ‘until the water itself seemed to burn’ (an extract from a story set in Vietnam, ‘The Lantern Festival’). What does the phrase ‘the water itself seemed to burn’ suggest, and how might it make the reader feel?
items.answer: the reflected lights are so bright and many that the river appears on fire, a magical, overwhelming image.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for an accurate meaning or connotation of ‘the water itself seemed to burn’; 1 for the effect on the reader, mood or idea created; 1 for a developed point that explores a second connotation or links to the wider text. Model point: the reflected lights are so bright and many that the river appears on fire, a magical, overwhelming image. Credit any valid interpretation supported by the words.

items.stem: Read ‘on the windowsills, on his mother’s sewing machine, on the leaves of the mango tree, even on his tongue’ from an extract from a story set in northern Ghana, ‘Harmattan’. Name the language feature, quote the key words and explain how they shape the reader’s response.
items.answer: Listing (‘even on his tongue’): the list builds to the most personal place, showing the dust gets everywhere.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for naming the technique (listing); 1 for selecting the key words ‘even on his tongue’; remaining mark(s) for analysis of the effect, e.g. the list builds to the most personal place, showing the dust gets everywhere.

items.stem: Explain why a writer might use flashback, as in: ‘As the plane lifted off, Mateo closed his eyes and was back in his grandfather’s workshop, the smell of sawdust thick in the air.’
items.answer: Flashback: the story moves back in time to an earlier memory.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: 1 for identifying flashback; further mark(s) for explaining the effect or clue: the story moves back in time to an earlier memory.

items.stem: Identify the structural technique and analyse how it affects the reader’s response: ‘Even now, forty years later, she cannot hear a train whistle without remembering the platform.’
items.answer: Flashback: the present-day narrator is about to recall a past event.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: 1 for flashback; remaining marks for analysis of effect on suspense, pace or understanding.

items.stem: Identify the structural technique and analyse how it affects the reader’s response: ‘Nobody noticed the small crack in the dam that morning. By the end of the week, everyone would wish they had.’
items.answer: Foreshadowing: it hints at a coming disaster, creating suspense.
items.markingKey: Award up to 3 marks from: 1 for foreshadowing; remaining marks for analysis of effect on suspense, pace or understanding.

items.stem: A story plan reads: A fishing village hears that a storm is coming. The fishermen argue about whether to go out one last time. One boat is caught at sea as the waves rise. The villagers light fires on the beach to guide it home. The boat returns and the village is united. Explain why the third event works as the climax, and suggest how the writer could build tension before it.
items.answer: ‘One boat is caught at sea as the waves rise.’ is the moment of greatest tension and the turning point; tension could be built through short sentences, a ticking clock, foreshadowing or delaying the outcome.
items.markingKey: Award up to 1 mark from: identifies why it is the turning point/greatest tension; a valid technique for building tension; credit for explanation.

items.stem: Explain your reasoning in each part. (a) Explain why ‘and then I woke up and it was all a dream’ is usually a weak ending. (b) Explain why a short story usually focuses on one main conflict.
items.answer: (a) It cancels the events and the reader’s investment, avoiding a genuine resolution of the conflict. (b) Limited length means one conflict can be developed fully, giving a clear shape and a satisfying resolution.
items.markingKey: (a) 1 mark: cancels events/cheats reader; 1 mark: no real resolution. (b) 1 mark: limited length; 1 mark: depth and clarity.

items.stem: These events from a story plan are in the wrong order. A: He tells her the story of her grandmother’s youth. B: She develops the last film and finds photos of a place she does not know. C: She travels to the place and meets an old man who recognises the photos. D: Lina takes a new photo in the same spot. E: Lina inherits her grandmother’s old camera. Put them in the order of a story mountain and label each stage.
items.answer: EBCAD: exposition (opening) – Lina inherits her grandmother’s old camera.; rising action – She develops the last film and finds photos of a place she does not know.; climax – She travels to the place and meets an old man who recognises the photos.; falling action – He tells her the story of her grandmother’s youth.; resolution – Lina takes a new photo in the same spot.
items.markingKey: Award up to 2 marks from: correct order EBCAD; labels exposition, rising action, climax, falling action, resolution.

items.stem: Write a complete short story with the title ‘Second Chances’. Plan a clear structure with a turning point and a satisfying ending. Write about 250–350 words.
items.answer: Model plan for ‘Second Chances’: exposition (character, setting, want); rising action (obstacle, complications); climax (turning point); falling action; resolution that links back to the title.
